title: Howell Homestead
summary: In 1657, houses were burned in Southampton village by two Shinnecock men and a black woman who served in one of the houses belonging to Eleanor Howell, widow of Edward Howell a founder of the town. The motive may have been in retaliation for the mistreatment of servants in the Howell home, or in response to roaming horses from Southampton destroying Shinnecock corn fields Colonial authorities in Hartford sent a troop of nineteen men under the command of John Mason, who commanded the massacre of the Pequot at.

why_this_matters: In 1657, two Shinnecock men and an African American woman allied together to burn the Southampton home of Eleanor Howell, actively protesting the mistreatment of servants and the destruction of Native cornfields by roaming English livestock. Examining this early act of coordinated resistance reveals how marginalized Indigenous and Black individuals forged powerful, multi-racial networks to fight back against the oppressive economic and ecological disruptions of colonization.
history_content: In 1657, several Shinnecock men and an African American woman conspired to burn down several buildings in the Southampton settlement. One of the buildings was the home of Eleanor Howell, widow of Edward Howell, who had helped found the town in 1640. One or more of the conspirators may have been servants in the Howell household, possibly retaliating for mistreatment or another conflict within the colonial household. The episode belongs to a wider period of tension, labor control, and colonial pressure in Southampton.
